title: Kyle Moore
text:
Personal Statement
Much of the discourse surrounding LLMs has focused on the fear (or for some, the hope) of replacement of humans. I am more hopeful and believe that AI’s true role will instead be one of collaboration. An important pre-requisite of effective collaboration is an understanding of the behavior exhibited by AI systems, which has been the primary focus of my research. To this end, however, I am interested in any research domain that promises to make AI open, understandable, and approachable to human users. This includes, but is by no means limited to, AI behavior, human-AI interaction, affective computing, and computational creativity.
Less professionally, I have a strong interest in a variety of fields, including philosophy, psychology, sociology, politics, and more. I hope, with time, to explore the increasingly substantial interactions between these fields and artificial intelligence. Please feel welcome to check out my About Me page if you are interested in more details about by personal history and interests.

title: Kyle Moore
text:
Selected Publications
Below are a selection of my recent research. To read about all of my publications, please check out this page

The Base-Rate Effect on LLM Benchmark Performance: Disambiguating Test-Taking Strategires from Benchmark Performance
Published in EMNLP 2024
This paper found that LLMs are strongly influenced by arbitrary token preferences that may confound and inflate benchmark performance. It also proposes a novel benchmark alteration technique, Nvr-X, that eliminates many such confounding biases for some benchmark types.
Chain of Thought Still Thinks Fast: APriCoT Helps with Thinking Slow
Published in CogSci 2025
Similar to the base rate paper above, this paper finds that chain of thought not only fails to eliminate some confounding biases, but may even exacerbate them. A novel alternative inferencing strategy, dubbed APriCoT, succeeds in modulating said biases while also improving task efficacy.
Investigating Human-Aligned Large Language Model Uncertainty
Published in FLAIRS 2026
This paper is the first work to investigate whether LLMs show similar uncertainty occurrence to humans.
Human-Alignment, Calibration, and Activation Patterns in Large Language Model Uncertainty
Under review
This paper extends on the work above to a much larger model and dataset pool, while also integrating uncertainty calibration and internal activation probing to better characterize the links between human and LLM uncertainty.

title: About Me
text:
Hi, and welcome to my webpage. My name is Kyle Moore, and I’m originally from the modest town of Munford, Tennessee, an exurb of Memphis. I kept busy through grade school and high school with extracurriculars, starting with sports (baseball and football) before transitioning into quiz bowl and working at the locally owned grocery store. Quiz bowl was easily my favorite aspect of high school, and I’m still proud to have placed second — alongside my teammates Jason DeWitt, Reiamarie Guevarra, and Jamie King — in the regional 2012 WREG Knowledge Bowl tournament. After graduating, I spent the next six years in Oxford, Mississippi, studying computer science at Ole Miss. I chose Ole Miss in part because I fell in love with the campus during the twice-yearly quiz bowl tournaments held there (a running theme, I know; I bet you can’t guess my favorite game show). Despite going in with no intention of doing so, I fell backwards into being a founding member of the Alpha Lambda chapter of Pi Kappa Phi, where I picked up leadership and social skills I badly needed at the time. Those skills were also sharpened during my tenure as an IT helpdesk technician for the University’s School of Business Administration under Sam Hammoud. Most importantly, Ole Miss is where I met my long-term fiancée, Mimi Truong (We’ve been engaged a while now — June 2020 turned out to be bad timing, and we’ll get around to it one of these days). We met while we were volunteering as moderators for that same twice-yearly tournament.
After a short but enlightening master’s program, I moved to Nashville, Tennessee to complete my PhD at Vanderbilt University. It was a rocky start, both because COVID hit at the end of my first year and because of limited research overlap with my first advisor, who, I must emphasize, is ultimately blameless. I soon found myself under the tutelage of Dr. Doug Fisher, who caught my interest with a tremendously inspiring seminar course called “Computation and Cognition.” I had the pleasure of working with Dr. Fisher for the remainder of my program, and I thank him heartily for his patience in staying with me through numerous health complications and a semi-retirement. With his help — along with the collaboration of my ubiquitous research partner, Jesse Roberts (now an Assistant Professor at Tennessee Tech University), and more undergraduate research assistants than I can name here - I completed my PhD in the late summer of 2026.
On a more personal note, I’ve always been drawn to fantasy and science fiction, whether in books, movies, video games, or anything else. As with many people in artificial intelligence, that was a clear inspiration for the path I’ve taken. Seemingly unlike many, though, I find a strong optimism in that media, buried beneath the pessimistic portents of annihilation. I see hope that we will create a machine as capable and impressive as what nature created in us, and that we will come out the other side having made new companions and collaborators, not conquerors nor chattel. Drawing on the stories that inspired me, I believe far more in Mass Effect’s Legion and Star Trek’s Data than in Skynet or Hal 9000. I recognize that day is likely far off, if it is realistic at all — even given the massive leaps we’ve witnessed during my PhD years alone — but I see it as a goal worth striving for in a world that is increasingly wary of AI advancement on one hand and overeager to replace human workers on the other.

Investigated whether and how large language models exhibit human-analogous patterns of uncertainty, drawing on cognitive science methodology to design controlled behavioral studies.
Studied test-taking artifacts and base-rate effects that confound benchmark-based evaluation of LLM capability.
Analyzed calibration and internal activation patterns underlying LLM uncertainty and their alignment with human judgment.
Extended artificial-population methodology to study psychological phenomena (e.g., strategic preference, categorization) in neural language models.
